title: Inside Meta’s push to put robots to work in data centers
content:
Meta is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers, and handle other tasks inside its data centers, according to several current and former workers familiar with the projects. The ongoing effort, which has not been previously reported, may eventually allow Meta to operate its rapidly expanding data center footprint with fewer humans, keeping labor costs in check as its spending on AI infrastructure soars.
Meta is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova, and ABB, according to the same workers, who asked to remain anonymous because they weren’t authorized to speak to the media. Kinova and ABB declined to comment. Watney didn’t respond to requests for comment.
In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could be used for power cycling or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a different robot to swap networking cables. One Meta data center worker estimates that if it’s successful, the bot could replace up to 80 percent of some people’s workloads. “We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,” says the worker. “It’s coming for us all, unfortunately.”
At some facilities, Meta quietly adopted another, relatively simple robot. It looks like a finger—or perhaps a pointy stick—that can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other device to restart it when remotely prompted by a human.
Meta declined to comment on the testing described in this story. Company spokesperson Francis Brennan said in a statement that Meta is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers. “America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II, and there’s a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,” he said.
But at a conference last year, Eric Xu, senior manager for robotics at Meta, said the company’s “long-term goals” are to put robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor the environment, and handle preventative maintenance. “We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start, otherwise we don’t have a chance to do this,” he said.
Until recently, robots largely weren’t well suited for the delicate work happening in data centers. They were expensive, and in earlier trials in the industry they sometimes crushed servers while attempting simple tasks, a person briefed on the experimentation says. But the hardware has gotten cheaper, and the AI models powering robots are now far more capable than they were a few years ago. Several startups are currently working to build commercial robots capable of assembling servers, swapping parts, and replacing wires.
Robots could offer more consistent output at a lower cost than human labor, especially in less populous regions where data centers are plentiful but qualified workers are scarce. Proponents also rally behind a pro-worker message: Like AI agents promise to do for knowledge workers, they argue robots could take on data center technicians’ most repetitive and dangerous tasks while freeing them to focus on more complex challenges. Longer term, getting workers out of the picture could make it more feasible to run data centers underwater, in space, or in other environments potentially inhospitable to living, breathing species.
“More and more of our customers are telling us ‘we want to run our data centers using humanoid [robots]’ because you can run them at higher temperatures, in the dark, and all these things,” says Paul Golding, who oversees so-called physical intelligence at the chipmaker Analog Devices.
The growing use of robots has received little attention from the activists driving a powerful nationwide movement against data centers. Tech companies often tout jobs for humans as an upside to the developments that can be used to justify tax breaks for them. In Altoona, Iowa, Meta operates what is now its largest data center campus, which employs hundreds of workers. The company opened the facility in 2014 and has several years left of a property tax break that allows it to save tens of millions of dollars annually, which the city has viewed as a worthwhile trade-off for having its cachet upped by having Meta jobs.
In Altoona, Meta worker group chats have taken on a demoralized tone, “saying we’re all going to be gone in a few years anyway because of the robots,” a person familiar with the discussions says. Even if adoption of robots proves slower than anticipated, some worry the quality of jobs available is trending downward. Two of the workers say that Meta is developing AI software and other technologies that they believe will allow it to hire lower-skilled—and thus, lower-paid—workers and centralize some roles in areas such as Denver, Colorado, that are more financially advantageous to the company.
“They no longer want people who can think independently, come up with creative solutions, or perform complex troubleshooting,” one Meta data center worker says. “They want ‘smart hands,’ people who are just capable enough to follow AI instructions and not mess anything up.”
Meta contends its need for skilled workers remains robust. This year, the company launched a long-term program to train thousands of people annually from any background in electrical, mechanical, and plumbing work at no cost to them. Meta is even guaranteeing employment in states such as Louisiana, Ohio, Indiana, and Texas for those who complete the training. It also partnered with building trade unions to fund apprenticeship programs.
But as communities rethink data center tax breaks and weigh putting new rules on the industry, the prospect of robots replacing at least some jobs may need to become a bigger concern. Altoona Mayor Dean O’Connor tells WIRED he hasn’t given much thought to robots taking jobs at Meta’s data center, though he frames automation as inevitable. “We will deal with it as it comes,” he says.
Tripping Cables
In a 2023 YouTube video, Meta touted that it was using a self-driving tugger robot to transport heavy server racks within its data centers as well as a wheeled, barcode-reading robot developed in-house to track inventory. The next year, Microsoft and Google unveiled separate investments in robots for their data center operations, and Amazon last year discussed using robots to help recycle parts at its facilities.
Pursuing robotics for “economically valuable tasks,” like “replacing a faulty server rack,” is “absolutely something we’re looking into at Microsoft,” Ashley Llorens, a managing director for the company’s research accelerator, tells WIRED.
Meta’s tugger and inventory robots are now operating in a number of the company’s data centers, including in Iowa and Virginia, according to the people familiar with the projects. They say the robots generally work well, though there are limitations.
The inventory bot is now also being used for failure inspections, but it can’t differentiate between green and red indicator lights on equipment because its camera only detects grayscale, meaning human checks are still required to assess some breakdowns. The device also struggles with corners and traversing the cables that are often in the path of its wheels. Because there aren’t that many of them, the robots need to be moved between buildings, which requires a door-opening human who maneuvers the robot with a remote control.
Two sources also describe the inventory bot as too slow. One says Meta previously explored using drones as a faster alternative, but ultimately didn’t pursue the idea.
Inside the Testbed
The Altoona data center campus is often where Meta prototypes new technologies. “What they do here in Altoona, they take to their other sites and put that in place there,” says O’Connor.
Since last June, Meta has been trying out a pair of dual-armed Watney robots for some cabling work at one of its Altoona

report.summary: Meta测试机器人执行数据中心任务，恐部分岗位被替代。
report.background: 随着AI基础设施投资激增，Meta数据中心的规模迅速扩大，传统人工运维面临成本高、技能短缺等挑战。机器人技术近年进步迅速，硬件成本下降，AI模型能力增强，使之成为可能。Meta在爱荷华州阿尔图纳等基地测试多种机器人，包括机械臂更换电缆、按电源键等。此前行业尝试曾因机器人压坏服务器而失败，如今技术已更成熟。同时，微软、谷歌、亚马逊也在探索类似应用，产业趋势逐渐明朗。但工人担忧失业，社区则未充分重视自动化带来的税收减免问题。
key_points: Meta正联合Watney、Kinova、ABB等厂商，在数据中心测试机械臂更换电缆、电源循环重启等任务，机器人应用范围不断扩大。
有工人估计机器人可替代部分岗位80%的工作量，引发基层焦虑，内部聊天群出现“大家都将失业”的悲观情绪。
机器人技术成熟是主因：硬件价格下降、AI模型能力提升，早期机器人会压坏服务器的问题已显著改善。
行业其他巨头同步布局：微软、谷歌、亚马逊已投资或讨论引入机器人，未来或支持高温、黑暗等人类不宜环境。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，数据中心机器人化将推动物理AI与基础设施运维结合，降低人力成本，但也引发就业结构变化。对开发者而言，机器人控制、计算机视觉和自动化运维技能需求上升，可能催生新的开发岗位与工具链。对普通用户而言，数据中心运维自动化有望提升服务稳定性和响应效率，但相关岗位缩水可能波及地方经济和就业，社区在税收减免谈判中需重新评估自动化带来的长期影响。
report.tools: 可关注Watney Robotics、Kinova、ABB等厂商的数据中心机器人产品，以及Meta自研的牵引车和库存机器人。开发者可学习ROS（机器人操作系统）和NVIDIA Isaac等机器人开发平台，留意后续可能开放的相关API和数据集。
